title: OSD UAP record 03_2024_DGI_Mission_Brief
what_is_it: An unclassified mission briefing from the All-Domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO) describing its structure, mission, achievements, analytic process, and three specific UAP case studies.
core_summary: This February 2024 AARO briefing outlines the office's four functional pillars — Operations, Science & Technology, Analysis, and Strategic Communications — and their key achievements. It defines UAP as anomalous detections not yet attributable to known actors, explicitly distinguishing them from unattributed balloon activity. The briefing presents three resolved or partially resolved UAP cases: a metallic orb in the Middle East (2022), equidistant objects over the western US resolved as likely commercial aircraft, and an object with an apparent wake over South Asia (2023) also resolved as a commercial airliner with video-compression artifacts.
interpretation_warnings: This is an official AARO briefing intended for departmental and congressional audiences; it reflects the office's institutional perspective and may understate anomalous findings.

Two of the three case studies were resolved as mundane (commercial aircraft with sensor or compression artifacts); the third (metallic orb) remains unresolved but showed no enigmatic capabilities — the selection may not be representative of the full case portfolio.
The document acknowledges severe data-paucity problems: many cases are unresolved not because they are anomalous but because there is simply not enough data to draw conclusions.
Collection bias toward military installations means the geographic and contextual distribution of reports does not reflect actual UAP distribution.
The briefing was last updated February 2024 but declassification review occurred on 2/5/2025, so there may be a gap between current AARO activities and what is described here.

public_headline: Pentagon UAP Office Briefing Explains Its Work and Three Case Studies
public_tldr: This February 2024 briefing from the Pentagon's All-Domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO) describes how the office is structured, what it has accomplished, and walks through three specific UAP cases — two of which were resolved as ordinary aircraft mistaken due to sensor quirks, and one (a metallic orb over the Middle East) that remains unexplained but showed nothing extraordinary.
public_narrative:
In February 2024, the All-Domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO) — the Pentagon unit responsible for investigating unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP) — prepared this unclassified mission briefing. The document was reviewed for public release on 5 February 2025 by the AARO Chief of Staff under authority granted by the FY24 National Defense Authorization Act. It lays out the office's four working areas: operations, science and technology, analysis, and public communications.

The briefing is notable for how it defines UAP: detections across air, sea, space, or multiple domains that cannot yet be attributed to a known source and that behave in ways sensors or observers do not readily understand. It explicitly states that UAP are not the same thing as unidentified balloons. AARO frames the existence of UAP as a direct consequence of gaps in the military's ability to monitor its own airspace and surroundings.

Three case studies are presented. In 2022, an MQ-9 drone observed what appeared to be a spherical, metallic object over the Middle East, consistent with other "metallic orb" sightings in the region. No unusual technical capabilities were observed, and the case remains in AARO's active archive without a firm explanation. The second case involved a P-3 patrol aircraft on a training mission over the western United States that spotted three objects spaced equally apart; air-traffic-control data showed they were likely commercial aircraft, and apparent shape changes turned out to be the sensor's autofocus adjusting. The third, from 2023 over South Asia, involved an MQ-9 observing an object that appeared to leave an atmospheric wake — analysis determined the object was a commercial airliner and the visible trail was caused by video-compression software overlaying one frame onto the next.

Beyond the case studies, the briefing acknowledges significant data problems. A large number of AARO's cases remain technically unresolved not because the objects are mysterious, but because there simply is not enough data to reach a conclusion. Over 100 reports were received from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), but most consisted of "lights" sightings with no detail on shape or behaviour. AARO also notes that its reporting is biased toward military bases and testing ranges because that is where its sensors and personnel are concentrated — commercial-pilot reporting is helping to broaden that picture. Only a very small percentage of all UAP reports display genuinely anomalous signatures.
public_caveats: Two of the three case studies were resolved as mundane (commercial aircraft misidentified due to sensor or compression artifacts). The third (a metallic orb) is unresolved but showed no extraordinary capabilities. These cases may not be representative of AARO's full portfolio.

Many cases remain unresolved not because they are unexplainable, but because there is not enough data — most FAA reports, for example, were simple 'lights in the sky' sightings with no detail on the object's shape or behaviour.
Reporting is heavily biased toward military installations and test ranges. The geographic spread of UAP reports reflects where the military operates, not necessarily where UAP occur.
This is an institutional briefing prepared for departmental and congressional audiences. It reflects AARO's own perspective and may understate anomalous findings.
The briefing was last updated in February 2024 but was not cleared for release until February 2025, so there is a one-year gap between the content and its publication.
